title: Noyack (Jessup's Neck)
summary: Noyack is associated with Noyack Bay, the hamlet now often spelled Noyac, and the long point or neck of land known as Jessup's Neck. The area also has archaeological evidence of long Indigenous use, including village and procurement-site contexts around Noyack.
map_geometry_source: Public orientation point for Jessup's Neck from OpenStreetMap/Nominatim; not an exact Noyack boundary or archaeological location.
why_this_matters: The archaeological remains of cooking hearths and dwellings at Noyack provide a tangible window into the daily domestic lives of early Indigenous coastal communities. Preserving the memory of this early village site reveals how Native peoples intimately mapped and utilized Long Island's distinct geographic features long before European settlement.
history_content: The placename brings together the Noyack Bay location, Jessup's Neck geography, older spelling forms, and related archaeological context. Dated source details appear in the historic moments below, where each event can carry its own reference.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Noyack, Noyak, Noiack, Noyac, and Nayack. The name is interpreted as a point or corner of land, a meaning consistent with its association with Jessup's Neck.

Why Place Names Matter

“Frozen in their time of creation, place-names reveal layers of the past from prehistoric times to the present.”

— Jon Nichol, Place-names and the National Curriculum for History (2014), Article opening paragraph
artifacts_content: Bone awls were common in the shallow holes used to cook food. It has been suggested that the awls were employed to pick up hot baked quahogs from the valves, as well as other hot foods, such as crab meat. Niantic cultural presence (from New England) was stronger here than on most of the eastern Long Island sites. Evidence of Sebonac cultural settlements were found on higher elevations, recognized as summer season occupation. Among the artifacts were remains of whelks, crabs, and summer species of fish. The most abundant winter food was the hard shell or quahog clam, with the soft shell clam second. Two mollusk species, usually rare on eastern Long Island, were found around the Noyack area. Among the western border of the site was a shell midden, mostly containing shell fragments and occasionally Niantic pottery sherds. Archaic origin projectile points were also found in the area. [1. Roy Latham, A Review of the Noyac Site, The Bulletin Number 20, 1960, pp. 3-5]
vandalism_content: A small six by six Niantic pot was found during a 1928 excavation by the Long Island Chapter of the N.Y.S.A.A. After leaving and returning in a one week period, the pottery was missing and later treated as lost. [1. Roy Latham, A Review of the Noyac Site, The Bulletin Number 20, 1960, pp. 3]
whereintheworld_content: Approximate general point at Jessup's Neck near Noyack Bay. The map placement is for orientation only, not an exact boundary for the hamlet, archaeological site, or seventeenth-century land descriptions.
